title: NYT Reports Trump Paid $750 in Federal Income Tax
description_short: The New York Times reported Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017.
description_medium: The New York Times reported that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and again in 2017, while claiming large business losses. The figures drew attention because they contrasted with the wealth and success he publicly projected. The reporting raised questions about how his finances were structured and what his tax records revealed.
description_long: A New York Times investigation published in September 2020 reported that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and another $750 in 2017, while his tax records showed large losses. The contrast between those reported payments and his public image as a wealthy, successful businessman intensified scrutiny of his finances. The report relied on tax information obtained by the newspaper; The newspaper described the figures as findings from tax information it obtained. The reported amount is evidence of what the newspaper found in those two years, not by itself a determination that a crime occurred. The episode became part of a broader debate about the complexity of the tax code, the ability of high-income taxpayers to offset income, and whether voters should have access to a presidential candidate’s financial records. The reported payments became a focal point in the public debate over Trump’s financial disclosures.

description_long: At a White House coronavirus briefing on April 23, 2020, Donald Trump asked whether light could be brought inside the body through the skin as a way to treat COVID-19. title: Oversight Board Upholds Facebook Suspension
description_short: Facebook’s Oversight Board upheld the suspension of Trump’s accounts while criticizing the indefinite nature of the penalty.
description_medium: Facebook’s Oversight Board upheld the suspension of Donald Trump’s accounts on May 5, 2021, but criticized Meta’s decision to make the penalty indefinite. The board said the suspension could remain while the company reconsidered it under a defined policy. The ruling affirmed the restriction while challenging how the platform had imposed it.
description_long: On May 5, 2021, Facebook’s Oversight Board reviewed the company’s suspension of Donald Trump’s accounts and upheld the decision to restrict them. The board also objected to the indefinite nature of the penalty, saying the company’s rules did not provide for an open-ended suspension in the way Meta had applied it. It gave the platform a period to reassess the measure and choose a defined, proportionate sanction. The decision therefore had two parts: it left the suspension in place at that time, while requiring the company to revisit how long and under what policy basis the restriction should continue. The board’s ruling focused on Facebook’s enforcement process and the indefinite duration of the penalty. The case drew attention to how a private social network handles the accounts of a prominent political figure and how an independent review body can scrutinize that decision. It was not a ruling by a court on Trump’s speech rights; it was a platform-governance decision about enforcement of Facebook’s own rules.

description_long: The Supreme Court announced on March 6, 2024, that it would hear oral arguments on April 25 in Donald Trump’s appeal asserting presidential immunity from criminal prosecution for conduct connected to his time in office. The dispute arose in the federal election-interference case, and the timing of Supreme Court review delayed the case from proceeding while the justices considered the threshold legal question. The case put questions about the scope of presidential authority and the operation of criminal law in tension, with practical consequences for the timing of a high-profile prosecution. title: Trump administration has still not settled on reasons for going to war with Iran
description_short: Trump administration has still not settled on reasons for going to war with Iran
description_medium: In the early days of the 2026 Iran conflict, the Trump administration gave changing explanations for using force. Trump cited Iran’s crackdown on protesters; Secretary of State Marco Rubio later warned that Iran might strike first and acknowledged Israel planned to act. The sequence left the public rationale unsettled, even as officials continued military operations.
description_long:
In the opening days of the 2026 conflict with Iran, the Trump administration offered several public explanations for its decision to use force. Trump initially pointed to Iran’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters as a reason for moving U.S. warships to the region. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said Iran could launch a preemptive strike. He then acknowledged that Israel was planning to strike first, and that the United States expected to be drawn into the conflict if it did not act.

The changing account left the public rationale unsettled. Whether Iran posed an imminent threat, whether U.S. action followed an Israeli decision, and what intelligence informed the timing are separate questions. Public statements do not establish what officials knew internally, but they determine how the administration explains military action to Congress and the public. The dispute over those explanations matters as the conflict expands and the administration seeks support for its objectives. The sequence does not by itself show that every stated concern was false; it does show that officials presented materially different reasons in rapid succession.

title: Trump tariff court ruling does little to end uncertainty for global business
description_short: Trump tariff court ruling does little to end uncertainty for global business

description_long:
The Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize Trump to impose the tariffs challenged in the case. The decision removed one legal basis for the administration’s trade measures, but did not prevent the government from seeking tariffs under other statutes. The White House said it would pursue alternative routes, which could take different amounts of time and may face separate legal challenges.

For companies trading across borders, the ruling did not settle what tariff rates would apply next or when. Importers and exporters had to consider the possibility of replacement measures while reviewing orders, prices, and supply arrangements. A representative of the British Chambers of Commerce said the decision did little to clear the “murky waters” for global business. The judgment resolved a question about executive authority under one law; uncertainty persisted because other legal authorities and future actions remained available. It did not invalidate every tariff or end the administration’s trade policy.

title: Trump: Half-truths and no truths: Trump’s latest claims on the UK factchecked
description_short: Trump: Half-truths and no truths: Trump’s latest claims on the UK factchecked
description_medium: Trump’s comments about the United Kingdom covered the Chagos Islands agreement, wind power, energy prices, and sharia courts. A fact-check examined his claims, including the length of the Diego Garcia lease and his remarks about the islands’ former residents. It also addressed his statements about wind turbines and North Sea drilling, separating verifiable details from his criticism of Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
description_long:
Trump’s comments about the United Kingdom focused on the Chagos Islands agreement, wind power, energy prices, and sharia courts. He criticized Prime Minister Keir Starmer and described the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius as an uncooperative decision. The agreement gives Mauritius sovereignty while leasing Diego Garcia, which hosts a major UK-U.S. airbase, to the United States and United Kingdom for 99 years. Trump referred to a 100-year lease and suggested Chagossians had not lived on the islands, though residents were forcibly removed decades ago.

He also called wind turbines “windmills” and urged more North Sea drilling. The UK government has emphasized renewable power partly to reduce exposure to volatile oil and gas prices. Trump’s claim that sharia courts adjudicate law in London was also misleading: sharia councils operate as community arbitration bodies without legal authority to decide cases. The fact-check compared each claim with the relevant agreement, energy policy, and legal arrangements, showing where his comments mixed a factual detail with an inaccurate or incomplete account.

title: Trump touts climate savings but new rule set to push up US prices
description_short: Trump touts climate savings but new rule set to push up US prices
description_medium: The EPA repealed the endangerment finding and vehicle greenhouse-gas standards. Trump said the change would save $1.3 trillion by 2055; the agency projected that amount in savings but estimated about $1.5 trillion in added costs from fuel, maintenance, insurance, and other effects. The competing estimates turned on the analysis’s assumptions, while the repeal removed a legal basis for federal climate rules.
description_long:
The Environmental Protection Agency finalized repeal of the endangerment finding, the legal basis for federal regulation of greenhouse-gas emissions, and ended vehicle greenhouse-gas standards. Trump said the change would save $1.3 trillion by 2055. The EPA’s regulatory analysis projected $1.3 trillion in savings from lower vehicle prices and reduced electric-vehicle spending, but also estimated about $1.5 trillion in added costs from fuel, maintenance, insurance, congestion, and other effects.

The analysis said gasoline could cost about 75 cents more per gallon by 2050 under the rollback. It also did not include the social and climate costs of additional emissions. Environmental advocates argued that the agency relied on an unrealistically low oil-price scenario to support its savings estimate. The dispute turned on the assumptions used to compare projected savings and costs, not just the headline figure. Repealing the finding removed a foundation for federal climate rules and vehicle standards, with likely consequences for emissions and consumer expenses over time.

title: Labor Union Decertification Campaign - Anti-Worker 'Right-to-Work' Expansion

description_long: Donald Trump implemented Project 2025's systematic campaign to 'weaken unions or make life tougher for them in at least a dozen ways' by facilitating decertification votes anytime union contracts are in force, eliminating project labor agreements, and promoting National Right-to-Work laws that allow non-union workers to benefit from union contracts without paying dues. Trump's anti-union campaign included facilitating decertification of labor unions for government contractors, making it easier to dissolve existing unions while protecting employers from accountability for wage theft and benefit violations through weakened enforcement mechanisms. The systematic labor destruction represented what construction unions called 'threat to the construction industry' that would eliminate prevailing wage standards, weaken health and safety protections, and allow exploitation of workers through contractor reclassification and reduced regulatory oversight.

title: COVID Death Toll Denial - 'It Is What It Is'

title: Trump administration has still not settled on reasons for going to war with Iran
description_short: Trump administration has still not settled on reasons for going to war with Iran

The downstream effects include elevated institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and measurable accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
In the opening days of the 2026 conflict with Iran, the Trump administration offered several public explanations for its decision to use force. Trump initially pointed to Iran’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters as a reason for moving U.S. warships to the region. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said Iran could launch a preemptive strike. He then acknowledged that Israel was planning to strike first, and that the United States expected to be drawn into the conflict if it did not act.

The changing account left the public rationale unsettled. Whether Iran posed an imminent threat, whether U.S. action followed an Israeli decision, and what intelligence informed the timing are separate questions. Public statements do not establish what officials knew internally, but they determine how the administration explains military action to Congress and the public. The dispute over those explanations matters as the conflict expands and the administration seeks support for its objectives. The sequence does not by itself show that every stated concern was false; it does show that officials presented materially different reasons in rapid succession.

description_long:
The Environmental Protection Agency finalized repeal of the endangerment finding, the legal basis for federal regulation of greenhouse-gas emissions, and ended vehicle greenhouse-gas standards. Trump said the change would save $1.3 trillion by 2055. The EPA’s regulatory analysis projected $1.3 trillion in savings from lower vehicle prices and reduced electric-vehicle spending, but also estimated about $1.5 trillion in added costs from fuel, maintenance, insurance, congestion, and other effects.

Environmental advocates argued that the agency relied on an unrealistically low oil-price scenario to support its savings estimate. The dispute turned on the assumptions used to compare projected savings and costs, not just the headline figure. Repealing the finding removed a foundation for federal climate rules and vehicle standards, with likely consequences for emissions and consumer expenses over time.

description_long:
CNN published an interactive review of Trump’s February 25, 2026 State of the Union address, placing annotations and fact checks alongside the speech. It covered taxes, tariffs, immigration, health care, energy, crime, Iran, and other subjects. The format let readers move through the remarks and examine specific claims in context.

One example addressed Trump’s assertion that he inherited inflation at record levels. Inflation was 2.9 percent in December 2024, Biden’s last full month in office, and reached 9.1 percent in June 2022, a 40-year high but not the highest rate in U.S. history. CNN also compared claims about economic growth with data showing 2.2 percent growth in 2025, below each year of Biden’s presidency. The review examined a speech delivered as Trump faced scrutiny over tariffs, immigration enforcement, and possible military action against Iran. It was a claim-by-claim fact-check, not a single conclusion about the address as a whole.
